summary: Defines two X.509 v3 certificate extensions, one binding IP address blocks to a certificate's subject and one binding autonomous system numbers. They convey the subject's authorization to use those resources.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3779 defines certificate fields that list the IP address blocks and network identifiers a key holder is allowed to use. A checker follows the certificate chain to make sure each delegation stays within the rights granted above it.

subtitle: Certificate extensions that record which IP address blocks and autonomous system numbers a key holder may use.

tldr.problem: A routing system needs a way to check whether an organization is authorized to use particular IP address blocks or autonomous system identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: Two X.509 v3 extensions list those resources in certificates. During path validation, each certificate's resources must fit within the issuer's resources.
tldr.outcome: The extensions let a relying system check delegated resource rights along a certificate chain. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 3779.

today: RFC 3779 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Certificates for Network Resources
sections.content:
RFC 3779 defines two extensions for X.509 version 3 certificates. One binds IP address blocks to the certificate subject's public key; the other binds autonomous system (AS) identifiers.

The extensions express a right to use the listed resources. The RFC describes a delegation chain from IANA through regional Internet registries and service providers to organizations. A routing protocol or registry can use the certificates to check authorization information.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can list the address blocks or network numbers that its key holder may use. The issuer must be authorized to pass those resources on.

sections.title: Encoding IP Addresses and Ranges
sections.content:
An IP prefix describes addresses that share the same leading bits. The extension encodes an address or prefix as a DER-encoded ASN.1 BIT STRING containing those fixed bits. A contiguous range that is not a single prefix is encoded with its lowest and highest addresses.

Encodings must be ordered, must not overlap, and must combine adjacent ranges whenever possible. A range that can be represented as a prefix must use the prefix form. These rules give each resource set a consistent, compact representation.
sections.plainLanguage: A prefix names addresses that share the same beginning. If a resource range does not fit one prefix, the certificate can list its lower and upper ends.

sections.title: The IP Address Extension
sections.content:
The IP address extension is identified by id-pe-ipAddrBlocks, with object identifier { id-pe 7 }. It groups resources by address family and can list prefixes or ranges for each group.

An entry can instead say inherit. This means the allowed addresses come from the issuer's certificate, continuing up the chain until a certificate lists explicit ranges. There must be one entry per address-family and optional sub-family combination, in ascending order.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP extension groups address permissions by address family. It can list specific ranges or tell the checker to use the issuer's permissions.

sections.title: The AS Identifier Extension
sections.content:
The AS extension uses id-pe-autonomousSysIds, with object identifier { id-pe 8 }. It can list AS numbers and routing domain identifiers, each as individual numbers or ranges.

AS entries must be sorted by increasing value, may not overlap, and contiguous values must be combined into a range when possible. An inherit choice takes the authorized identifiers from the issuer's certificate. The extension does not change how AS identifiers are managed.
sections.plainLanguage: The second extension lists network identifiers instead of IP addresses. It can name individual numbers, ranges, or permissions inherited from the issuer.

sections.title: Checking a Certificate Path
sections.content:
When a certificate path is checked, each certificate's IP resources must be contained within the corresponding resources in its issuer's certificate. The same rule applies to AS identifiers. Validation must fail if a certificate claims resources its issuer did not authorize.

The trust-anchor certificate and every certificate in the path must contain the relevant extension. The initial permitted resource set comes from the trust anchor.
sections.plainLanguage: Each certificate can pass on only resources it was given. If one claims more than its issuer allowed, the checker rejects the certificate path.

sections.title: Security and Authorization
sections.content:
X.509 certificates are digitally signed, so the RFC says the extensions need no additional integrity service and the certificates do not need to be secret. Their main security purpose is to express authorization to use IP addresses or AS identifiers.

In the secure BGP context described by the RFC, the certificate acts as a capability: possession of the corresponding private key is tied to the listed resources. The subject name is therefore largely irrelevant to this authorization check.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate's signature protects its contents from change. For these extensions, the key question is whether the key holder has permission to use the listed resources.
